title: Harnessing gasotransmitters for orthopaedic infection therapy: Mechanisms and advanced delivery platforms
abstract: Orthopaedic infections are increasingly prevalent in the aging population, posing a significant clinical and economic burden. Despite progress in antimicrobial therapies, challenges such as antibiotic resistance and superbug emergence persist. Gas therapy has emerged as a promising strategy for managing orthopaedic infections. Classical gasotransmitters-including nitric oxide (NO), carbon monoxide (CO), and hydrogen sulfide (HS)-exhibit antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects at controlled concentrations, though improper dosing may induce adverse effects. This review critically examines the dual mechanisms through which gasotransmitters combat infection while promoting orthopaedic regeneration. We also survey advanced delivery platforms-such as smart scaffolds, nano-reservoirs, and on-demand release systems-engineered for targeted gasotransmitter delivery to infected bone tissue. Finally, we discuss current limitations and future prospects, aiming to inspire novel biomaterial designs for targeted therapeutic delivery and to advance gas therapy as a viable option for orthopaedic infection treatment.

title: Bioprinted core-shell living material platform for spatially controlled encapsulation of Bacillus subtilis and sustained metabolite exchange
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents an escalating global health crisis, demanding alternative strategies to reduce resistant pathogen burden across environments. Microbe-based biocontrol is promising, yet effectively deploying it in practical settings remains challenging. In this study, we present a 3D bioprinted core-shell construct featuring a polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) shell with tunable nanoscale porosity, encapsulating germinable spores of the biocontrol agentTH035. This configuration supports long-term spore viability while providing protection from common environmental stressors including UV-C irradiation, ethanol exposure, and desiccation over 4 weeks. The nanoporous PEGDA shell enables effective bacterial confinement while facilitating sufficient metabolite exchange forgermination and growth, as well as suppression of methicillin-resistant(MRSA) growth by approximately one order of magnitude. This approach demonstrates the feasibility of embeddingspores within engineered scaffolds for extended competitive functionality. The versatility and scalability of digital light processing (DLP) based bioprinting offers significant potential for tailored designs and high-throughput manufacturing. This proof-of-concept platform may find future applications in areas such as biomedical packaging, environmental sanitation, and built environment surface coatings, particularly in settings where intermittent moisture or nutrient availability can support spore germination and biocontrol activity.

title: Artificial intelligence catalyzes antimicrobial peptide design
abstract: With broad-spectrum, low resistance, and multifunctional properties, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising therapeutic agents against drug-resistant pathogens, yet their discovery and optimization still remain challenging due to the complexity of sequence-function associations. Artificial intelligence (AI), through the construction of comprehensive data-driven models that assisted with miscellaneous learning strategies, enables de novo peptide design by learning latent representations inherent in peptide sequences as well as their biological properties to ensure physically plausible and biologically relevant predictions. Consequently, this paradigm enhances the likelihood of designing peptide candidates with significantly improved therapeutic potential, reducing resource-intensive trial-and-error processes and revealing the transformative impact of computational innovation in advancing next-generation therapeutics. Here, we provide a snapshot of this field and survey two modes of AI-driven technologies for AMP design, one concentrated on identifying whether current data possess antimicrobial activity (identification-oriented) and the other on generating AMP candidates with potential therapeutic properties (generation-oriented). We also highlight the challenges and limitations that still hinder AMP development even accelerated by AI, as well as the foreseeable prospects, from finer-grained explorations to model-driven data enrichment and model enhancement.

title: Antifungal mechanisms of volatile organic compounds and lactic acid produced by Lactiplantibacillus pentosus and their biocontrol application in fresh corn against Fusarium graminearum
abstract: Fusarium graminearum causes cereal spoilage and mycotoxin production. Currently, biocontrol microorganisms have emerged as a safe and promising strategy to manage the contamination of toxin-producing fungi in cereal grains. The primary objective was to elucidate the antifungal mechanism of an isolated strain of Lactiplantibacillus pentosus Q11 against F. graminearum and to evaluate the preservative effects of its cell-free supernatant (CFS) in fresh sweet corn. In vitro antifungal assays of L. pentosus Q11 showed strong antagonistic activity against F. graminearum, Aspergillus flavus, and Penicillium expansum, as well as the ability to reduce zearalenone. Moreover, whole-genome analysis revealed no genes related to virulence and antimicrobial resistance, and no hemolytic activity was observed, which suggested the potential safety of strain Q11. Moreover, the CFS of L. pentosus Q11 effectively inhibited the mycelial growth of F. graminearum, disrupted hyphal integrity, and induced fungal cell death. Moreover, 3 organic acids and 38 volatile compounds in the CFS of Q11 strain were identified by SPME-GC-MS and HPLC, in which 2-nonanone, 2-methylpyrazine, lactic acid, acetic acid were predominant compounds. The CFS and lactic acid combined with 2-nonanone severely damaged hyphae of F. graminearum, by disrupting cell membrane and wall, leading to leakage of intracellular substances, showing a synergistic antifungal effect of the two vital compounds. Subsequently, the treatments of CFS and combined agents significantly decreased 88.05% - 89.52% of fungal populations, and AFBand DON mycotoxin accumulation in fresh sweet corn after 12 days of storage compared to the control. The malondialdehyde content in the treated corn was decreased by 29.25% - 31.50%, consistent with the higher activities of POD and APX, thereby preserving their sensory attributes and nutritional quality. Metabolomic analysis revealed that L-glutamate, γ-glutamylcysteine, and oxidized glutathione were significantly downregulated in the glutathione metabolism pathway in the treated corn, indicating that CFS containing lactic acid and 2-nonanone could repress fungal growth and alleviate oxidative stress in fresh sweet corn. Overall, these findings demonstrate that L. pentosus Q11 with synergistic volatile organic compounds and lactic acid is a promising biocontrol agent in preserving fresh sweet corn.

Bacterial competence and genetic diversity: Implications for the design of diagnostics and vaccines
abstract: Bacterial competence and genetic diversity are key determinants of microbial evolution, directly influencing pathogen adaptability, diagnostic reliability, and vaccine effectiveness. Natural transformation, together with horizontal gene transfer and homologous recombination, enables rapid genomic remodeling, facilitating the acquisition of antimicrobial resistance, modification of diagnostic targets, and generation of antigenic variants. These processes are particularly prominent in naturally competent and highly recombining pathogens, where population structures range from clonal to panmictic, shaping responses to selective pressures such as antibiotic use and immunization. This review synthesizes current understanding of the mechanisms governing bacterial competence and their role in generating genomic diversity, with emphasis on implications for diagnostics and vaccine design. Case studies-including,, and-illustrate how recombination-driven diversification contributes to serotype replacement, diagnostic escape, and variable vaccine performance. Emerging approaches, including pan-genomic target selection, high-throughput sequencing, CRISPR-based diagnostics, and next-generation vaccine platforms, offer strategies to address these challenges but remain constrained by genomic variability and limited global surveillance. We argue that integrating evolutionary dynamics into diagnostic and vaccine development is essential for sustaining effectiveness. Continuous genomic monitoring and adaptive design frameworks will be critical to anticipate and mitigate competence-driven bacterial evolution in clinical and public health settings.

title: Health Diplomacy in Limited-Resource Settings in Africa: What It Takes Towards a Realistic, Resilient and Equitable Agenda?
abstract: Health diplomacy (HD) in African nations is often characterized as limited settings due to resource scarcity, weak governance and fragmented health systems. Although HD is crucial for addressing the continent's interconnected health challenges, including endemic diseases, infectious threats, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), climate change, persistent conflicts and foundational weaknesses, its effectiveness is frequently undermined by the structural persistence of hidden power, a legacy of colonialism that controls agenda-setting and perpetuates dependency. Drawing on decolonial theory, this article argues that a purely technical application of HD is insufficient. It proposes a strategic framework for HD implementation that builds long-term resilience and sustainability. Achieving a realistic agenda requires a commitment to local ownership and co-leadership, health systems strengthening (HSS) and context-specific adaptation. Simultaneously, an equitable agenda must proactively tackle power imbalances, prioritize a rights-based approach and enhance local agency in diplomatic negotiations. By strategically linking health initiatives to broader security/development goals (smart power) and framing health as a fundamental human right, this framework enables HD to transition from a mechanism that risks reinforcing inequalities to a powerful tool for achieving resilient, sustainable, and truly equitable collective health security.

title: WasteFams: a database of protein families from global wastewater microbiomes
abstract: Wastewater surveillance has emerged as a critical tool for global epidemiology, yet the functional diversity of wastewater microbiomes remains poorly characterized at the protein level. Here, we present WasteFams, the first comprehensive database dedicated to the systematic exploration of protein families in wastewater metagenomic and metatranscriptomic studies worldwide. Integrating data from 580 metagenomes, 132 metatranscriptomes, and 1709 reference genomes (504 metagenomes, 129 metatranscriptomes, and 1151 reference genomes after filtering), WasteFams catalogs 3887 non-redundant protein families (containing ⪰100 members) derived from over 105 million predicted proteins. Each protein family is enriched with multi-layered annotations, including AlphaFold3 structural predictions, taxonomic classifications, and biome-specific metadata. To further expand their functional annotation, we integrated deep genomic context analysis to link protein families to mobile genetic elements, biosynthetic gene clusters, antibiotic resistance genes, and CRISPR elements. Accessible through the EnvoFams portal, WasteFams provides a user-friendly interface featuring advanced search capabilities, sequence and structural similarity tools, and interactive visualization modules. As global initiatives increasingly leverage wastewater for public health and environmental insights, WasteFams can serve as a critical resource for discovering novel microbial functions, monitoring resistance mechanisms, and exploring the biotechnological potential of secondary metabolites within wastewater-engineered ecosystems.

title: Genomic characterization of Aliarcobacter spp. from livestock in commercial and smallholder farms and from children in Ghana and Tanzania
abstract: spp. are emerging foodborne pathogens posing public health risks through zoonotic transmission in agricultural settings. Characterizing their phylogenetic relatedness, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), and virulence factors is critical for assessing their impact on food safety and health in Ghana and Tanzania. We collected 144isolates (139 from farm animals and 5 from human clinical cases) and analyzed their genomes using molecular phylogenetics, antimicrobial resistance gene (ARG) profiling, and virulence gene identification. Phylogenetic analysis confirmedas the predominant species with two distinct subclades exhibiting multiple drug resistance. Notably, we identified a second clade ofthat may represent a novel species. Additionally, a potential new subspecies withinwas detected, supported by genomic and digital DNA:DNA hybridization (dDDH) analyses. A multiple antibiotic-resistantisolate was found to harbor a resistance plasmid encoding five AMR genes. The pangenome reflected an open genome structure with a vast accessory gene pool related to resistance and virulence. ARGs conferring tetracycline, macrolide, and aminoglycoside resistance were widespread, with commercial farm isolates showing higher resistance burdens than those from smallholder farms. Virulence genes varied, illustrating broad genetic diversity and adaptive potential. This study highlights genomic plasticity and emerging resistance inspp. from human and animal sources in sub-Saharan Africa. The discovery of new clades and a resistant plasmid underscore the need for enhanced One Health surveillance to control the spread and impact of these pathogens on public health and food safety.

title: Cross-kingdom antimicrobial resistance profiling: A unified multiplex PCR assay for simultaneous bacterial and fungal detection
abstract: Antimicrobial-resistant (AMR) pathogens have emerged as a critical global health concern, necessitating the development of rapid and reliable screening tools. Conventional culture-based identification is labor-intensive and often delays appropriate antimicrobial therapy. This study aimed to develop and validate a multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay for the simultaneous detection of methicillin-resistant, carbapenem-resistant, and fluconazole-resistant. Initially, monoplex PCR was performed to evaluate the specificity and sensitivity of each primer set targeting(bacterial identification),(methicillin resistance),(carbapenem resistance),(fungal identification), and(azole resistance). Based on these results, multiplex PCR was developed to simultaneously detect multiple target pathogens within a single reaction. The assay successfully amplified all target genes, and no cross-reactivity was observed. Furthermore, multiplex PCR enabled the rapid, simultaneous detection of multiple AMR pathogens within a single reaction. A prototype multiplex PCR kit was also developed based on this study. Collectively, these findings indicate that the developed multiplex PCR assay has potential as a feasible approach for the simultaneous detection of AMR pathogens.

title: Anthropocentric Thinking about Antibiotic Resistance and Ecosystems: Relations between Explanations and Misconceptions in American Undergraduates from Urban and Rural Backgrounds
abstract: Intuitive conceptual frameworks can shape students' reasoning for biology concepts, sometimes forming misconceptions. Anthropocentric thinking-reasoning that centers humans-often relates to misconceptions about antibiotic resistance and ecosystem change. Cultural influences, such as lifestyles with greater exposure to nature, have been associated with reduced anthropocentric reasoning. The backgrounds of rural and urban children vary in opportunities for experiences with nature-rural children have greater exposure and urban children less exposure to outdoor settings. The relationship between students with rural and urban backgrounds and anthropogenic thinking highlights potential differences in students' biology misconceptions. Here, we compare students' rural and urban backgrounds and institutions to their use of anthropocentric reasoning and its relatedness with misconceptions in biology. Students from rural and urban backgrounds were recruited to complete a survey with written and categorical agreement ratings for misconceptions in biology. All students-regardless of hometown population and institution densities-showed similar rates of anthropocentric reasoning. However, the use of anthropocentric language was highly correlated with biological misconceptions. Our research suggests that anthropocentric thinking is pervasive in undergraduate students and influences biological misconceptions.

Extended spectrum beta lactamases and carbapenemase-producing Escherichia coli in humans, animals and the environment in East Africa: a scoping review
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is escalating in East Africa through close human-animal-environment interactions. Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBL) and carbapenemase-producingare clinically critical pathogens, yet local evidence is limited. This scoping review synthesizes evidence on ESBL and carbapenemase-producingin East Africa to inform One Health AMR control strategies. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, PubMed and Scopus were searched, identifying 279 records published between 2015 and 2025. After removing duplicates and screening, 185 articles were assessed for eligibility; 154 studies spanning human, animal and environmental sources met the inclusion criteria. Two reviewers independently extracted epidemiological, microbiological and molecular data in Covidence, including resistance genes and transmission evidence. The 154 included studies spanned 11 East African countries, led by Ethiopia ( = 55), Tanzania ( = 39) and Uganda ( = 22). Most studies (85.7%) were cross-sectional and human-focused (68.2%), with only 19 (12.3%) using a multi-sector One Health design. Overall, 21,554isolates were recovered from 74,700 samples. ESBL prevalence was reported in 117 studies (76.0%, median 46.8%) and carbapenemase prevalence in 65 (42.2%, median 3.3%), representing heterogeneous study-level estimates.predominated (89.9%), led by(26.1%); reported carbapenemase genes included,,andWhole-genome sequencing in 30 studies (19.5%) identified high-risk clones ST131, ST10, ST38 and ST410, though animal, food-chain and environmental sectors remained underrepresented. This review maps the current evidence on landscape for ESBL/carbapenemase- producingin East Africa, highlighting gaps in surveillance that are largely due to heterogeneity of available genomics data and limited longitudinal data within the "One Health" sectors. We recommend scaling up genomic capacity and standardized longitudinal surveillance to better understand national and regional AMR transmission and MDRinfections.

title: Dietary licorice improves carcass yield, hepatocellular protection, gut health, oxidative status, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens
abstract: Over the past decade, phytotherapy such as licorice has attracted research as an alternative to antibiotic growth promoters in broiler production, driven by rising concerns over antimicrobial resistance. However, the consistency of its effects across productive, physiological, and health outcomes remains inconsistent. This meta-analysis quantitatively synthesized published experimental evidence on the effects of dietary licorice on growth performance, carcass yield, blood indices, visceral organs, oxidative status, intestinal morphology, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens. A systematic literature search identified studies published between 2010 and 2025, and effect sizes were computed (Hedges'; 95% confidence interval). Pooled estimates were derived under the random-effects model using the restricted maximum likelihood estimator, with between-study heterogeneity characterized bythe-statistic. Univariable mixed-effects meta-regression was conducted to identify study-level moderators of treatment response, and publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot and the Rosenberg fail-safe N criterion. Dietary licorice did not affect feed intake or the feed conversion ratio, but it did increase body weight gain (BWG; SMD = 0.289; = 0.002), breast, thigh, gizzard, and bursa weights ( < 0.05). Gut integrity also improved with the villus height/crypt depth ratio (SMD = 0.931; = 0.041), andspp. counts (SMD = 0.266; = 0.003) increased, whilepopulations were suppressed (SMD = -1.737; < 0.001). Overall, the findings support that licorice enhances body weight gain, with route, duration, sex, and strain moderating efficacy.

abstract: ()is a globally pervasive and economically significant pathogen in bovine intramammary infections (IMIs) and is responsible for both clinical and subclinical mastitis. This study systematically investigated the global epidemiology offrom bovine IMIs, addressing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) amongthrough a meta-analysis. A total of 143 studies published between 2000 and 2025 were identified through comprehensive searches, which were based on predefined inclusion criteria. The data were systematically extracted, and the statistical analyses were performed in R (v4.5.2). The meta-analysis included 143 studies (145,457 samples), with a pooledprevalence of 24.78% and high heterogeneity (I = 99.51%). Subgroup analyses demonstrated significant heterogeneity in prevalence by study design, publication year, and region, with greater heterogeneity in cross-sectional studies (I>95%, < 0.001). Meta-regression identified sample size as a significant source of heterogeneity (β = -0.00002, = 0.02; R = 3.41%). The highest prevalence was reported in Cameroon (67%), Sri Lanka (64.3%), Indonesia (57%), and India (44%), with the lowest prevalence reported in Poland (0.7%), Taiwan (2.0%), Australia (5.5%), and New Zealand (5.3%). AMR was highest for doxycycline (70.7%), penicillin (65.2%), and ampicillin (62.8%); moderate to oxacillin (44.6%) and vancomycin (40.2%); and lowest for gentamicin (27.5%) and amikacin (18.3%). is highly prevalent in bovine IMIs worldwide, with marked regional heterogeneity and substantial resistance to commonly used antimicrobials, emphasizing the urgent need for targeted surveillance, prudent antimicrobial use, and improved mastitis control strategies at the global and regional levels.

N-acetylcysteine as an adjunct to antibiotics against bacterial biofilms: A systematic review of in vitro evidence
abstract: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is investigated as an antibiotic adjunct, but acidity, formulation and experimental context complicate interpretation. We evaluated comparative in-vitro evidence while distinguishing biofilm prevention, established-biofilm treatment and resistance evolution. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science were searched through August 2026, with supplementary searching. Extraction distinguished NAC preparation and exposure pH, medium, hydrodynamics, NAC-alone controls, treatment intent and interaction methodology. Results were synthesized by experimental context, regimen, phase and endpoint without pooling or whole-study efficacy voting. Fifty-five studies were included: 7 evaluated combination exposure during formation only, 37 after establishment only, 9 both, and 2 resistance evolution. NAC-alone arms were documented in 39 studies, partial or formulation-specific in 9, and not identified in 7. Only two studies included a continuous-flow model. Selected combinations improved biofilm-associated outcomes, but intrinsic-acidic and neutralized preparations, biomass and viability endpoints, and planktonic versus biofilm interaction tests were not interchangeable. Liposomal and catheter-lock findings differed by dose matching, isolate and control set. Polymyxin findings varied with organism, resistance background, medium and exposure; rifampicin-alone and rifampicin-containing multidrug comparators addressed different questions. NAC is a context-dependent experimental adjunct, not an established class-wide antibiotic potentiator. The evidence does not support clinical antibiotic dose reduction or routine NAC combination therapy. Translation requires controlled final exposure pH, matched monotherapy and formulation controls, clinically relevant background regimens, viable-burden and regrowth outcomes, and resistance monitoring.

Combating antimicrobial resistance through multimodal data via artificial intelligence
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health challenge, leading to substantial mortality and economic losses without science-based interventions. Conventional approaches to combating AMR have important limitations in addressing this escalating threat. Recent advances in AI, including deep learning, large language models, and protein language models, provide new opportunities to integrate multimodal data for AMR research. However, evidence remains uneven, with many approaches limited to computational benchmarking rather than real-world validation. Here, we critically review AI applications in AMR, focusing on rapid diagnosis, therapeutic discovery, and clinical decision support. AI-based diagnostic models can identify resistant pathogens and predict resistance profiles, but most lack prospective clinical evaluation. AI-assisted drug discovery and alternative therapies have generated promising candidates, although most remain at computational, in vitro, or early preclinical stages. Large language models may support decision-making, but their clinical use remains preliminary. Successful translation of AI into clinical and One Health practice will require representative datasets, independent validation, prospective evaluation, and robust governance.

Moreover, reports of antimicrobial resistance among bacteria isolated from mastitic goats are scarce. In Ethiopia, treatment decisions for mastitis largely rely on empirical clinical experience rather than routine antimicrobial susceptibility testing. To address this gap, a cross-sectional study was conducted from November to December 2024 in Waghimra, Amhara, Ethiopia, to identify the major bacterial causes of mastitis and to evaluate their antimicrobial susceptibility patterns. Strengthening One Health Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance in Bangladesh: Insights from the Fleming fund country grant
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an escalating global public health concern, with particularly severe implications for low and middle-income countries such as Bangladesh. In Bangladesh context, fragmented surveillance systems and the extensive use of antimicrobials across human, animal, and aquaculture sectors contribute to the rapid emergence and spread of resistance. Strengthening integrated surveillance through a One Health approach is therefore crucial to support effective policy development and response strategies. This review outlines the policy, implementation, and key outcomes of the Fleming Fund Country Grant in Bangladesh between 2020 and 2025. It draws upon multiple data sources, including programme reports, routine AMR surveillance data, laboratory capacity-building initiatives, and stakeholder engagement activities across human, animal, aquaculture, and environmental sectors. Through this initiative, a coordinated national AMR surveillance network was established, comprising 20 laboratories across multiple sectors, including three designated national reference laboratories. The initiative strengthened surveillance through the introduction of standardized protocols and SOPs, improved diagnostic capacity, skilled workforce, and implementation of laboratory quality assurance systems, including EQA and NEQA. These measures enhanced the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of AMR surveillance data. In addition, the establishment of a national AMR data integration platform facilitated real time data sharing and evidence-based decision-making. A total of 208,346 bacterial isolates were analyzed, with AST results reported to the AMR dashboard across the human, and animal, health sectors. Overall, the Fleming Fund programme has made a substantial contribution to strengthening integrated AMR surveillance in Bangladesh by operationalizing a One Health framework. Continued political commitment, increased domestic investment, and the institutionalization of surveillance systems will be essential to sustain these gains and ensure long-term resilience against AMR.

Microfluidic-assembled curcumin ionizable lipid nanoparticles enhance aqueous delivery and antibiofilm activity against Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance and biofilm-associated infections demand novel therapeutic strategies. Curcumin is a natural polyphenol with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity; however, its clinical utility is fundamentally constrained by negligible aqueous solubility and limited biofilm penetration. Here, we used microfluidic assembly to prepare curcumin-loaded ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cur@LNP) with three clinically established ionizable lipids (SM-102, MC-3, and ALC-0315). The resulting formulations were uniform, with hydrodynamic diameters of approximately 90 nm and polydispersity indices near 0.1. Relative to free curcumin in DMSO, Cur@LNP lowered the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) 8-fold and the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) 16-fold against planktonic, and markedly reduced viable biofilm-resident cells at matched concentrations. Scanning electron microscopy showed that Cur@LNP treatment remodeled mature biofilms into irregular, debris-rich aggregates with reduced extracellular matrix coverage. Notably, antimicrobial performance was indistinguishable across the three structurally distinct ionizable lipids at every concentration tested. Within this in vitro, single-strain system, the antibiofilm effect is therefore dominated by the cargo (curcumin) rather than by ionizable-lipid chemistry, and it is most likely attributed to enhanced aqueous solubilization of curcumin rather than to engagement of the lipid headgroup with the biofilm matrix. These results position microfluidic-assembled ionizable LNPs as a reproducible, scalable solubilization platform for poorly water-soluble natural antimicrobials.

title: Metagenomic analysis of commensal small mammal samples from an international cargo shipping area, Bangkok Port, reveals potential zoonotic pathogens and implications for One Health surveillance
abstract: Commensal small mammals, such as rats and shrews, are recognized reservoirs for numerous zoonotic pathogens; however, their role in pathogen circulation at transport hubs remains underexplored. This study employs shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize microbial communities and assess zoonotic potential in tissue samples from commensal small mammals captured at Bangkok Port, an international cargo shipping hub in Thailand between June and August 2025. Following host read depletion, taxonomic profiling was performed to identify bacterial taxa of public health relevance, including sequences assigned tospp.,,, and. The virulence factor and antibiotic resistance gene profiles revealed that some of these pathogens have pathogenic potential and are related to drug-resistant bacteria. In addition,was identified as a shared taxon among rats, shrews, and their associated fleas. The findings support the ecological roles of mammalian hosts and their ectoparasites as reservoirs for pathogens of public health concern. These results emphasize the need to strengthen surveillance programs for commensal small mammals to monitor and mitigate the spread of transboundary pathogens at international maritime gateways.

Wild boar as a sentinel species for ecosystem health surveillance: A review
abstract: Sentinel surveillance uses selected species that are widely distributed, easily sampled, and exposed to multiple health threats as indicators of ecosystem health. The Eurasian wild boar () is a broadly distributed game species that meets these conditions. We conducted a systematic review to assess the suitability of the wild boar as a sentinel or indicator species for monitoring health hazards relevant to ecosystem health, focusing on the hazards monitored, methods, justification for use, perceived performance, limitations, and proposed improvements. We identified 86 studies explicitly framing the wild boar as a sentinel species, covering a wide range of hazards, including 30 pathogens, 44 environmental contaminants, two biological toxins and 13 antimicrobial resistance (AMR) indicators. It was used to monitor pathogens (57%), environmental contaminants (31.4%), AMR (12.8%), and biological toxins (3.5%). Research effort was concentrated in Europe (84.9%) and relied mostly on hunted animals (90.7%). Wild boar were frequently selected as sentinels due to their previous use as indicators of ecosystem health in the literature, omnivorous diet, wide distribution, and accessibility as game species. However, hunting-based sampling may introduce biases, while post-mortem conditions and ecological variability may affect results. Despite this, 74.4% of studies supported their use as sentinels, particularly for pathogens and environmental contaminants. In contrast, their perceived suitability for AMR was more variable, and no quality assessment was available for biological toxins. Overall, wild boar sentinel surveillance is considered logistically efficient and valuable for monitoring ecosystem health hazards. However, its effectiveness is context-dependent and influenced by methodological and ecological limitations. Improving surveillance design through systematic sampling, alternative sample sources (e.g., found-dead animals or non-invasive methods), integration of multi-species data, and inclusion of covariates could enhance the reliability of findings within a One Health framework.

title: Global spread of carbapenem-resistant Providencia driven by high-risk lineages and plasmid co-evolution
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant(CRP) is a formidable opportunistic pathogen with extensive drug resistance, posing an increasing threat to human, animal, and environmental health. However, its global genomic epidemiology and resistome-plasmidome co-evolution within a One Health context remain poorly understood. Here, we conducted a comprehensive population genomic and plasmid analysis of 1197 CRP isolates from 35 countries spanning 2012-2025. We reclassified the CRP population into ninespecies, identifyingandas established epidemic species alongside the rapid emergence ofand. We pinpointed 2019 as a critical inflection point, marking the transition from endemic stability to rapid global epidemic expansion (80.8% isolates in 2019-2025). Ten intercontinentally disseminated high-risk sequence types (e.g., ST46, ST79), each with strict species-ST specificity, were responsible for global spread. Thegene (62.4% prevalence) was the predominant carbapenem gene, exhibiting strong geographic and species specificity and mutual exclusion with other major carbapenem genes. Plasmids encoded approximately 80% of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes, with 78.0% of these plasmids belonging to 75 stable clusters. These clusters evolved a dual specialist-generalist strategy, with the broad-host-range cluster 72 mediating interspecies AMR transmission and cluster 7 acting as a super-vector carrying six carbapenem genes. Importantly, CRP circulated across interconnected human, animal, and environmental reservoirs, with distinct host-associated species distributions suggesting ecological niche adaptation and potential cross-host dissemination of resistance determinants. These findings demonstrate that the global expansion of CRP is driven by the combined evolution of high-risk clones and mobile genetic elements across interconnected ecological sectors, underscoring the need for integrated One Health surveillance and coordinated interventions spanning clinical, veterinary, agricultural, and environmental settings.

title: Management of pneumonia by the emergency radiologist
Exploring veterinarian and pet owner perspectives on the risk of antimicrobial resistance when feeding raw meat diets to dogs
Prevalence and genomic characterization of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium across a duck breeder-hatchery-grow-out production system in China
Five years of wastewater surveillance reveal COVID-19-Associated amplification and seasonal shifts in bla (KPC) and bla (NDM)
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has intensified in recent years, raising concerns about the potential impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on AMR dynamics. However, the influence of pandemic on the enviromental occurrence and dissemination of antibiotic-resistant genes (ARGs) remains under investigation. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) provides an integrated view of community-level AMR dynamics, yet long-term assessments spanning the pandemic period remain limited. This study investigated the occurrence, temporal patterns, and seasonal behavior of two clinically relevant carbapenemase genes,and, in raw wastewater from the Attica region over a five-year period (July 2021-September 2025). A sensitive and specific 3-plex qPCR assay was developed and analytically validated for the simultaneous quantification of,, and 16S rRNA, the latter serving as a stable bacterial load indicator. Across the monitoring period,was consistently detected, showing a steady increase and reaching its highest concentrations in 2023, whileexhibited intermittent but pronounced surges, particularly in 2023. Comparison with community SARS-CoV-2 viral loads suggest temporal association with AMR signatures in wastewater. Seasonal analysis showed non-uniform patterns, with atypical warm-season peaks of both ARGs in 2023-2024 and a return to classical autumn-winter peaks in 2025, suggesting a gradual restoration of pre-pandemic seasonality. To our knowledge, this is among the first long-term WBE studies to characterize post-COVID-19 shifts in ARG occurrence and seasonality. The results demonstrate that the pandemic period was associated with elevated and fluctuating ARG levels in the urban wastewater system, emphasizing the need for sustained AMR monitoring. These findings address critical knowledge gaps in environmental AMR surveillance and support the integration of WBE into public health strategies aimed at mitigating AMR dissemination.

title: Prevalence of antimicrobial-resistant Escherichia coli as an indicator bacterium in livestock and companion animals in Mongolia
Genomic epidemiology to investigate the origins and zoonotic implications of antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli on beef and lamb meat sold by independent butchers in Wales
abstract: Many studies have identified antibiotic resistant (ABR)on meat. Appropriate hand hygiene and cooking practices should minimize the risk of gastrointestinal colonisation with ABRfound on meat, and the subsequent chance of causing resistant opportunistic extraintestinal infection. There are large gaps in our understanding of the prevalence, origins and zoonotic potential of ABRfound on meat, however, and particularly for meat reared in extensive farming systems. Wales is a devolved nation within the United Kingdom having large populations of extensively-reared sheep and beef cattle. To help address knowledge gaps around ABRon extensively reared meat, therefore, beef mince and lamb loin/leg steaks/chops were purchased from 50 (beef) and 46 (lamb) independent butchers across Wales. Following enrichment culture, 200 g meat samples were found to be positive forresistant to amoxicillin (31% positivity), streptomycin (28%), spectinomycin (29%), amoxicillin-clavulanate (11%), 3rd generation cephalosporins (2%) and fluoroquinolones (5%). Phylogenetic analysis confirmed that Welsh lamb meat ABRisolates ( = 78) are more closely related to those found in faecal samples collected around sheep ( = 352) than around beef cattle ( = 361) on Welsh farms. This suggests that faecal contamination at or around slaughter is their primary origin. We found no closely related meat/infection clones (<20 SNPs distant and the same antibiotic resistance genes) when comparing ABRfrom Welsh meat ( = 91) and those causing extraintestinal infections in people ( = 2387) in an English region bordering Wales. We conclude, therefore, that the wider zoonotic implications of finding ABRon beef and lamb meat sold at independent butchers in Wales are small, though a more geographically and temporarily contemporaneous survey is warranted to address this further.

title: Genomic insights into activated antimicrobial resistance of in situ hospital-wastewater biofilm

Sewage surveillance for assessing clinical antibiotic resistance prevalence: Combining metagenomic and phenotypic data
abstract: Surveillance of antibiotic resistance in clinical isolates is a cornerstone for the management of bacterial infections but is limited in large parts of the world, often due to lack of resources. Sewage surveillance has been proposed as a promising, resource-efficient complement to the traditional surveillance approach based on samples from many individual patients. Both phenotypic data on resistance in sewage isolates and abundance of antibiotic resistance genes in sewage have been shown to correlate with resistance prevalence in clinical isolates. Here, we aimed to directly compare and combine an isolate-based and a gene-based sewage surveillance approach to evaluate what best can reflect clinical resistance rates. The two approaches, based on susceptibility testing of collectedisolates and metagenomic sequencing, respectively, were applied to municipal sewage samples collected in ten European countries. The data generated was related to available data on resistance to aminopenicillins, fluoroquinolones, third generation cephalosporins and aminoglycosides prevalence in clinicalisolates using beta regression models. None of the tested individual predictors were superior across all four investigated classes of antibiotics. For modelling of aminopenicillin resistance, a clearly higher Rvalue was obtained when isolate-based and gene-based data was combined as predictors, also after adjusting for the number of included variables. We conclude that there could be a value of including both isolate- and gene-based sewage data for predictions of resistance rates in clinical isolates, while emphasizing the value of linking predictors to specific species and classes of antibiotics.

title: Clonal diversity, virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes of Enterococcus faecalis and Klebsiella pneumoniae from urban rats in Malaysia
abstract: Peridomestic rats serve as important carriers of zoonotic pathogens, including multidrug-resistant bacteria such asand. However, information on the clonal diversity, antibiotic resistance, and virulence of these pathogens in wild urban rats remains limited, particularly in tropical settings. This study investigatedandin urban rats from wet markets across four Malaysian states. A total of 277 rats (, = 177;, = 100) were trapped, and lung tissues were processed for bacterial isolation. Isolates were identified by 16S rDNA sequencing and examined for antibiotic susceptibility, resistance genes, and virulence factors using PCR. Clonal relationships were determined through multilocus sequence typing (MLST). Nineteenand sevenisolates were recovered. Allisolates carried multiple virulence factors (,,, and), and four tetracycline-resistant isolates possessed,, and. Five novelsequence types (ST730 - ST734) were identified. Allisolates carried the SHV gene; two also harbored FOX, and two possessedandvirulence factors. Two novelSTs (ST2641 and ST2642) were detected. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that both species displayed diverse sequence types scattered across global lineages. These findings suggest that urban rats may act as potential carriers of virulent and antibiotic-resistantand. These findings support the inclusion of urban rats in future One Health surveillance programs investigating antimicrobial resistance and virulent bacterial pathogens.

Copper-coated carbon nanotube surfaces for inhibiting biofilm formation by Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Biofilm-associated infections caused by clinically important pathogens such as() and() remain a major challenge in healthcare settings due to enhanced antimicrobial resistance and persistence. In recent years, copper-coated carbon nanotubes (Cu-CNTs) have gained considerable attention as promising antimicrobial nanomaterials for preventing biofilm formation on medical devices and hospital-associated surfaces. This review summarizes recent advances in the development and application of Cu-CNT-based antimicrobial coatings, with an emphasis on their antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens. The synergistic combination of the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of CNTs and the potent antimicrobial properties of copper (Cu) ions enhances microbial inhibition. Previous studies suggest that Cu-CNTs interfere with initial bacterial adhesion, inhibit biofilm maturation, and disrupt established biofilms through mechanisms involving oxidative stress generation, membrane destabilization, and cellular damage. Furthermore, the review discusses the physicochemical characteristics, antimicrobial mechanisms, biomedical applications, and potential challenges associated with Cu-CNT coatings, including toxicity and biocompatibility concerns. Overall, Cu-CNT-based coatings represent a promising strategy for developing durable antimicrobial surfaces to control chronic biofilm-associated infections and reduce healthcare-associated contamination.

Differential modulation of gentamicin antibacterial activity by vitamin B12 and vitamin D3 against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria: an in vitro-in silico study
Antibiotic resistance genes in aquaculture: Molecular detection, environmental dynamics, and biological control strategies
abstract: Antibiotic resistance in aquaculture is a major threat to sustainable fish production and global public health. This review provides a comprehensive and critical synthesis of studies on antibiotic resistance in aquaculture published between 2005 and 2025, identified through a systematic and reproducible literature search. It clarifies the molecular basis of resistance, characterizes the environmental distribution of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), and evaluates current and emerging control strategies in aquaculture systems. Evidence is organized into thematic domains encompassing molecular mechanisms, environmental reservoirs and drivers, diagnostic and surveillance tools, and biological alternatives to antibiotics. In parallel, vaccines, probiotics, and bacteriophage therapy show promising, context-dependent potential when embedded in multifaceted biocontrol frameworks. This review highlights priorities including protocol standardization, rapid farm-deployable diagnostics, and optimized synergistic biocontrol strategies, supported by artificial intelligence and big data analytics, to facilitate a transition from reactive treatment to preventive, system-level resistance management in aquaculture.

title: Bridging soil resistome and clinical inference: A four-tier evidentiary framework
abstract: Soils support a varied range of microbial communities and are important repositories of antimicrobial resistance genes. Sequence-based techniques, such as quantitative polymerase chain reaction and shotgun metagenomics, have substantially aided soil-resistome cataloging. Nevertheless, discovery alone does not indicate activity, transferability, exposure, or clinical relevance. This review contends that better clinical inference requires tying presence-based signals to function, mobility, and exposure routes, rather than just increasing survey volume. We offer a four-tiered evidentiary paradigm that distinguishes between detection, functional or expression-based evidence, mobile genetic element context, and exposure-linked evidence in environmental, animal, and human compartments. Because activity, mobility, and cross-compartmental similarity support several claims, layered, claim-aligned approaches are required for careful One Health interpretation.

title: Harnessing hydrogel technology for advanced periodontitis therapy: A multifunctional approach to oral health restoration
abstract: Periodontitis is a bacterially driven inflammatory disease that can lead to tooth mobility and tooth loss. Conventional non-surgical therapy, antibiotics, and surgery may be limited by residual subgingival biofilms, antimicrobial resistance, and variable clinical outcomes. This review synthesizes recent studies of hydrogel-based systems for local periodontal therapy, focusing on stimuli-responsive release mechanisms, cargo-loading approaches, and regenerative outcomes in relevant animal models. Across these studies, hydrogels function as localized delivery matrices that can prolong retention at periodontal defects, regulate therapeutic exposure, and support tissue repair. We further evaluate translational considerations, including degradation behavior, long-termstability, and immunocompatibility. These findings position hydrogels as adaptable platforms for more precise periodontitis management and identify priorities for preclinical optimization before clinical translation.

title: Microbiota-constrained bacterial density limits phage infection in the gut and allows persistence of susceptible cells
abstract: With the rise of antibiotic resistance, bacteriophage-based treatments against bacterial infections have regained momentum. However, phage therapy has so far shown only moderate success in complex environments like the mammalian gut, where phages are particularly promising tools for microbiome engineering and specific elimination of opportunistic pathogens. Here, we use different murine models of intestinal colonization to quantitatively assess the minimal population size of susceptiblecells that is required for phage replication in the gut (replication threshold). We found that the composition of the intestinal microbiota is a key factor shaping phage-bacteria interactions by restricting the carrying capacity of susceptible host cells. We further demonstrate that the replication threshold enables coexistence of susceptible and resistant bacteria in phage-treated mice, with implications for phage-based applications in complex environments like the gut.

Omni-ARMD: an integrated genomic and clinical knowledgebase bridging clinical phenotypes and molecular determinants of antimicrobial resistance
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat, yet its molecular determinants remain difficult to characterize in real-world settings, as genomic and clinical data are fragmented across resources. Existing databases typically separate gene-level mechanisms, curated genotype-phenotype associations, and large-scale clinical antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) data, limiting cross-scale interpretation. Here, we present Omni-ARMD, an open-access knowledgebase that integrates multi-source genomic and clinical data to systematically infer genotype-phenotype relationships in AMR. Omni-ARMD bridges large-scale clinical AST records and gene-level resistance evidence through a confidence-weighted log-odds enrichment framework, which quantifies genotype-phenotype associations at the organism-antimicrobial level and integrates these associations into aggregated cross-domain evidence representations. The current release includes over 12 million de-identified microbiology records from more than 1 million patients, harmonized to generate over 7.83 million standardized AST records. It also integrates over 0.36 million gene-phenotype associations, spanning 38 organisms, 52 antimicrobials, and 375 resistance genes. Omni-ARMD links over 5.16 million clinical records to genomic evidence, achieving a 65.86% match rate and a 2.61% coverage of organism-antimicrobial pairs. Omni-ARMD provides interactive modules for clinical investigation, genomic evidence analysis, mechanistic interpretation, and artificial intelligence-assisted exploration, enabling integrative and data-driven discovery in AMR. Omni-ARMD is freely available at www.omniarmd.cn.

title: Thirteen years of environmental surveillance of ESKAPE organisms and Escherichia coli in an equine hospital: Informing infection control
abstract: Bacteria from the ESKAPE group (i.e., Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterobacter species) and Escherichia coli are frequently multidrug-resistant and can be associated with healthcare-associated infections, an increasing concern for veterinary settings. To determine the environmental prevalence of ESKAPE and E. coli on surfaces which can act as reservoirs of infection in clinical areas in equine hospitals. Observational study. Routine environmental sampling was performed in one busy equine hospital with Swiffer® wipes to screen surfaces from high-risk areas (e.g., surgical theatres, intensive care unit [ICU], isolation unit), equipment (e.g., endotracheal tubes) and high-touch areas (e.g., keyboards) following selective species-specific protocols for each target organism. Monitoring hand-hygiene of hospital staff and students was by hand-plate sampling. After a pilot phase E. faecium was excluded from routine screening. Nine hundred and ninety-five environmental and hand-plate samples were collected from April 2010 to February 2023. The overall E. coli-SKAPE (E. coli, methicillin-resistant S. aureus [MRSA], K. pneumoniae, A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa and Enterobacter spp.) prevalence was 37.9%, where E. coli was the most (and K. pneumoniae the least) common target organism identified (18.0% and 1.7% respectively). E. coli was most prevalent in general stables and yards (37.7%) and offices (25.7%). Enterobacter spp. was the main organism in the environmental samples from ICU (24.2%) and isolation unit (22.9%, along with E. coli). Concerningly, hand-plate sampling showed that MRSA was the most common organism detected on hands (8.4%), followed by A. baumannii (5.2%) and E. cloacae (3.9%); however, E. coli, P. aeruginosa and K. pneumoniae were not found in these samples. Inconsistent sampling limited longitudinal analysis. We generated baseline environmental contamination data and demonstrated high E. coli-SKAPE hospital surface and hand contamination, informing infection control to prevent environment-to-patient cross-transmission.

title: Acupuncture Mediates the Treatment of Childhood Pneumonia via Modulation of Lung ADRB2
abstract: Childhood pneumonia (CP) remains a major cause of pediatric hospitalization and mortality. Antibiotic resistance and drug-related adverse reactions highlight the need for safe adjunctive treatments. The β₂-adrenergic receptor (ADRB2) is associated with airway reactivity and inflammatory responses. Acupuncture has been reported to modulate autonomic and immune functions; however, its precise molecular mechanism in CP remains unclear. Clinical outcomes were evaluated alongside transcriptomic analyses and animal experiments. The transcriptomic analyses comprised a pediatric PBMC dataset (GSE261482) and an independent mouse lung RNA-sequencing dataset (GSE325662). An LPS-induced juvenile mouse model was established to assess lung pathology, inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-10), and ADRB2 expression. Salbutamol and ICI-118551 were used to examine ADRB2-related effects. Acupuncture showed significant adjunctive benefit, improving day-5 efficacy (P = 0.001), day-7 efficacy (P < 0.001), and day-5 clinical scores (P = 0.002), while shortening hospital stay (P < 0.001) without serious adverse reactions. Transcriptomic analysis implicated adrenergic signaling, particularly ADRB2, in CP. In juvenile mice, acupuncture reduced lung inflammation and modulated cytokine levels and ADRB2 expression. These findings suggest an association between ADRB2-related signalling and the pulmonary inflammatory response to acupuncture. Acupuncture was associated with improved clinical outcomes in CP and attenuated lung inflammation in an LPS-induced juvenile mouse model. ADRB2-related adrenergic signaling may be involved in this anti-inflammatory effect. These results support the potential role of acupuncture as an adjunctive intervention for CP, although further studies are needed to confirm the causal contribution of ADRB2 and to define the underlying cell-specific mechanisms.

title: Long-term effect of low ciprofloxacin concentration on nitrogen removal performance, enzymatic activity, microbial community and antibiotic resistance gene of sequencing batch reactor
abstract: Ciprofloxacin usually exists at low concentration in surface water and wastewater. In this research, the nitrogen removal, enzymatic activity, antioxidant response, microbial succession, functional gene and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) of sequencing batch reactor were investigated under long-term exposure of 100 μg/L ciprofloxacin. The NH-N removal efficiency almost unchanged during 188-day operation. However, the ammonia-oxidizing rate, nitrite-oxidizing rate, nitrate-reducing rate and nitrite-reducing rate decreased by 17.34 %, 18.38 %, 24.98 % and 38.81 % on day 188 by comparison with 0 µg/L ciprofloxacin, respectively. Similarly, the activities of ammonia monooxygenase, nitrite oxidoreductase, nitrate reductase and nitrite reductase decreased by 25.76 %, 27.79 %, 30.65 % and 39.81 %, respectively. The increase of antioxidant enzymatic activity under long-term ciprofloxacin stress eliminated excess reactive oxygen species to alleviate oxidative damage. The relative abundances of Nitrosomonas, Nitrosospira, Nitrobacter and Nitrospina decreased with the increase of operation time. The relative abundances of nitrogen-removal key genes (e.g., amoA, nxrA, narG and nosZ) decreased with the increase of operation time, as well as the key enzymes in TCA cycle with their encoding genes. The total abundance of the top 30 ARGs increased by 7.57-fold by comparison with 0 µg/L ciprofloxacin, especially for efflux pump genes. The enrichment of ARG-encoded efflux pumps and antioxidant defense competed for the limited electrons and ATP, which led to an energy/electron trade-off with nitrogen metabolism. The present results are helpful to deeply understand the linkage among the nitrogen removal, microbial community and resistance genes under long-term exposure of low antibiotic concentration.

title: UV-aged tire wear particles and their leachates jointly enhance antibiotic resistance gene dissemination
abstract: Tire wear particles (TWPs) represent a major source of environmental microplastics, yet how ultraviolet (UV) aging influences their effects on the transfer of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) remains unclear. Here, the promoting effects and underlying mechanisms of UV-aged TWPs and their leachate on bacterial conjugative transfer were investigated. Aging significantly increased the specific surface area and oxygen-containing functional groups of TWPs, and promoted the release of heavy metal ions and organic additives into leachate. In conjugation assays, 60-day-aged TWPs enhanced the transfer frequency of plasmid RP4 by 15.3-fold; whereas the corresponding leachate alone caused a 62.0-fold increase. Mechanistically, aged TWPs acted primarily as a physical oxidative stressor, promoting conjugative transfer through reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and disruption of cell membrane integrity. Aged leachate acted mainly as a chemical signaling stressor, inducing biofilm formation and collective behavioral responses that created a protective microenvironment conducive to plasmid exchange, although they also contributed to oxidative stress. Combined exposure further produced a response greater than that of either pathway alone, establishing a physicochemical dual-stress framework that drives ARGs transfer. Collectively, these findings suggest that environmental aging critically shapes the ecological risks of microplastics, positioning aged TWPs as potential vectors for ARGs dissemination and underscoring the need to consider both particle-associated and leachate-mediated pathways in future risk assessments.

title: LysBM39, a novel T4-like lysozyme with antibiofilm activity against streptococcal pathogens associated with bovine mastitis
abstract: Bovine mastitis is one of the major causes of economic losses in dairy production worldwide and is mainly caused by bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus agalactiae and Streptococcus uberis. The ability of these bacteria to form biofilms contributes to persistent infections, antimicrobial resistance, and treatment failure. Although bacteriophages have emerged as promising alternatives to antibiotics, their application is limited by factors such as narrow host range and reduced activity in complex matrices such as milk. In this context, phage-derived proteins expressed heterologously may overcome some of these limitations. In this study, the phage-derived lysin LysBM39, containing a T4-like lysozyme domain, was heterologously expressed, and evaluated for its antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against bovine mastitis isolates. Growth inhibition assays were performed using 17 S. uberis and 23 S. agalactiae isolates, while biofilm formation assays were conducted with S. agalactiae isolates. LysBM39 significantly reduced the growth of 7 out of 17 (41.2%) S. uberis isolates, with reductions ranging from 13% to 31% compared with untreated controls. No growth inhibition was observed for S. agalactiae, even at higher enzyme concentrations. However, the recombinant protein significantly reduced biofilm formation in 8 out of 17 (47.1%) S. agalactiae isolates, with reductions ranging from 54% to 79%. These findings demonstrate the potential of LysBM39 as an alternative or complementary antimicrobial strategy for controlling bovine mastitis pathogens, particularly through its antibiofilm activity.

title: Quinoclamine, a repurposed agricultural algicide, functions as a multi-target quorum sensing inhibitor to attenuate Pseudomonas aeruginosa virulence and potentiate antibiotic efficacy
abstract: The widespread overuse and misuse of antibiotics have precipitated a global antimicrobial resistance crisis, compounded by a dwindling pipeline of novel antibiotic discovery. As the quorum sensing (QS) system tightly mediates bacterial colonization and pathogenicity in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, QS-targeted anti-virulence therapy has emerged as a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics. In this study, through an integrated approach combining virtual screening and systematic experimental validation, we identified quinoclamine as a candidate QS inhibitor and comprehensively characterized its anti-virulence efficacy via in silico, in vitro, and in vivo assays. Molecular docking analysis predicted that quinoclamine simultaneously interacts with three core QS regulators: LasR, RhlR, and PqsR. In vitro experiments demonstrated that quinoclamine significantly inhibited key QS-controlled virulence factors including pyocyanin and extracellular proteases, as well as biofilm formation and bacterial motility, without affecting bacterial growth. Quantitative real-time PCR confirmed that quinoclamine downregulated QS-associated virulence genes and competitively blocked autoinducer-receptor binding. Furthermore, quinoclamine exhibited synergistic bactericidal activity with five clinical anti-pseudomonal antibiotics. Additionally, quinoclamine has moderate disruptive capacity against pre-formed mature biofilms, and partially potentiates the bactericidal efficacy of ciprofloxacin against sessile bacteria embedded within biofilms. The in vivo protective efficacy was validated across three infection models: C. elegans fast-killing, C. elegans slow-killing, and mouse acute pulmonary infection. Impressively, the combination of quinoclamine and 1/2 × MIC ciprofloxacin further improved host survival in all three models and reduced bacterial burden in mouse lung lesions. Collectively, these findings characterize quinoclamine as a promising QS inhibitor with broad anti-virulence activity, and provide robust experimental support for the development of QS-targeted anti-virulence therapies against P. aeruginosa infections.

title: Bacillus subtilis R-179 combined with Enterococcus faecium R-026 alleviate antibiotic-associated diarrhea by modulating gut microbiota and antibiotic resistance genes
abstract: Although probiotics are known to be effective against antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD), it remains unclear how they regulate gut microbiota and resistance genes to exert this effect. This study investigated the effects of live combined Bacillus subtilis R-179 and Enterococcus faecium R-026 (LCBE) on AAD, gut microbiota and resistance genes in C57BL/6 mice. Twenty-four male C57BL/6 mice were divided into three groups. The M and LCBE groups were administered 0.2 mL of antibiotics (550 mg.kgamoxicillin, 450 mg.kgclindamycin, and 400 mg.kgstreptomycin) twice a day for twenty-five consecutive days. The N group was provided normal saline. After successful modeling, the LCBE group was gavaged with LCBE at a dose of 0.02 g/mice/day for nine days. LCBE significantly improved multiple diarrhea-related parameters, reduced the levels of lipopolysaccharides, TLR4, and IL-6, increased the levels of IL-10, Occludin, and ZO-1, and alleviated inflammatory infiltration and mucosal damage. It increased the abundances of Bifidobacterium_pseudolongum and Lactobacillus_johnsonii, and decreased the abundances of [Clostridium]_innocuum, Clostridioides_difficile, and Klebsiella_pneumoniae. Furthermore, it reduced the levels of various resistance genes, including APH (3'')-Ib, QnrS1, sul1, and sul2, increased the levels of betaine and indoxyl sulfate, and decreased the levels of 4-chlorophenyl and taurocholic acid. During the treatment of AAD, LCBE alleviated inflammation, repaired intestinal damage, modulated the composition of gut microbiota and expression of drug resistance genes, and improved serum metabolism in the treatment of antibiotic-associated diarrhea. These findings underscore the potential therapeutic significance of LCBE as a multi-target agent to manage AAD.

title: Genomic microdiversity of Mycobacterium africanum in Sénégal
abstract: Mycobacterium africanum is responsible for up to half of tuberculosis cases in West Africa and comprises four sub lineages. Its genomic diversity remains undescribed in Sénégal where M. africanum was first described and where the present study was conducted. Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) identified one M. africanum lineage L5 isolate and 50 M. africanum lineage L6 isolates, with a predominance of sub lineage L6.1.1 (24/50, 43.7%) across seven of eight regions of Sénégal. The Dakar region gathered all the sub lineages (L5.3, L6.1, L6.1.1, L6.1.3, L6.2.3, L6.3.1, L6.3.2, L6.3.3, unclassified L6), except for sub lineage L6.2. Further Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) analysis revealed substantial genetic diversity among the lineage L6 isolates with mean value of 668.54 (±239.61), while themedian was 465 SNPs (interquartile range = 400, median absolute deviation:163.09). According to the World health Organization Catalogue of mutations in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex and their association with drug resistance, WGS predicted antibiotic resistance in 16 strains. Comparing Drug Susceptibility Testing (DST) and WGS results showed complete concordance across 19 DST tested strains. This study highlights the diversity of M. africanum in Sénégal, with intra-lineage genomic variability and predicted antimicrobial resistance. The presence of synonymous mutations in the absence of resistance-associated variants suggests that WGS-based predictions of drug resistance should be interpreted with caution.

title: Burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance associated with modifiable human antibiotic consumption: An observational study
abstract: Human antibiotic use is widely believed to contribute to the evolution and maintenance of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in bacterial pathogens. While antibiotic stewardship should thus discourage use in situations where AMR-related harms outweigh clinical benefit, evidence to inform this assessment of tradeoffs is lacking, most notably in low-resource settings where gaps in antibiotic access persist. Quantitative understanding of use-resistance relationships is thus necessary as countries navigate commitments from the 2024 UN General Assembly resolution to reduce AMR burden by 2030. We used global surveillance data on AMR prevalence from 2000 to 2018 representing over 30 million bacterial isolates from 114 countries, along with antibiotic consumption estimates for each country and year, to estimate elasticity relationships between AMR and antibiotic exposure. Our analyses addressed 16 bacterial pathogens and antibiotic consumption across 7 drug classes, controlling for country-level health and development indicators via weighted regression models. Across pathogens, evidence that AMR is associated with population-level antibiotic exposure is strongest for Acinetobacter spp., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Escherichia coli. In a modeled counterfactual scenario, we estimate that 10% lower levels of antibiotic use, in comparison to current levels, across classes, would be associated with 38,000 (95% confidence interval: 36,000-41,000) fewer annual deaths attributable to AMR globally. Although substantial, this total represents only 0.50% of estimated bacterial disease mortality. In sub-Saharan Africa, where risk of death due to bacterial disease is greatest, the modeled avertible burden of AMR-attributable deaths comprises only 0.34% of bacterial disease mortality. Key limitations of the study include reliance on ecological relationships to infer modifiable burden, and under-representation of low-resource settings in surveillance data on antibiotic consumption and AMR. Our findings suggest near-term achievable reductions in AMR-attributable deaths may be modest relative to the persisting burden of bacterial disease mortality. These estimates should inform assessments of the potential benefits and harms of restrictive versus permissive antibiotic use paradigms in epidemiologically distinct settings.

title: Staphylococcus warneri MN336185 from Fermented Rice Water: a Multifunctional Probiotic with Anti-pathogenic and Longevity Benefits in C. elegans
abstract: Fermented ecosystems serve as critical reservoirs for functionally diverse microorganisms with applications in food safety and nutraceuticals. This study focuses on Staphylococcus warneri MN336185 (SW), a non-traditional probiotic strain isolated from fermented rice water and evaluating its probiotic and bio-preservative properties. SW demonstrated significant gastrointestinal and oxidative stress tolerance, high epithelial cytocompatibility (> 80%), non-hemolytic safety, and an exceptional cholesterol assimilation efficiency of 85%. Moreover, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) confirmed genomic biosafety, establishing the absence of acquired enterotoxins, superantigens, ica-dependent biofilm determinants, and most transmissible antibiotic resistance elements. Studies on the host-microbe interface confirmed strong adherence of SW to HT-29 cells with proportionate competitive anti-adhesion potential against Salmonella enterica and Escherichia coli. The strain could also upregulate tight-junction proteins, claudins and zona occludens, indicating barrier-protective effects. In Caenorhabditis elegans, supplementation of SW as live feed enhanced lifespan, pharyngeal pumping, locomotory abilities, and resistance to pathogens. Further, challenge tests involving incorporation of live cells or cell-free supernatant of SW into rice-based matrices resulted in significant, time-dependent reduction of pathogens with a 4 log₁₀ CFU decrease during refrigerated storage. Collectively, these observations could establish S. warneri MN336185 as a multifunctional probiotic strain with potential application in functional food and natural biopreservation strategies.

title: The Evolving Landscape of Neonatal Care and Research : Based on 14(th) Dr. I. C. Verma Excellence in Research Award Delivered as Oration on 4(th) October 2026
abstract: Neonatology has undergone a remarkable transformation over the past six decades, evolving from a discipline focused predominantly on preventing neonatal death to one increasingly concerned with quality of survival, neurodevelopment, family-integrated care and long-term health. Despite substantial progress, neonatal mortality remains a major global health challenge. In 2024, approximately 2.3 million newborns died globally, with the highest mortality rates in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. India has achieved a substantial decline in neonatal mortality, from 28 to 17 per 1000 live births between 2015 and 2023, accompanied by rapid expansion of facility-based newborn care. However, prematurity, low birth weight, intrapartum complications, infection, antimicrobial resistance, inequitable access, workforce constraints and inadequate long-term follow-up remain major challenges. The epidemiology of neonatal disease is also changing, with increasing survival of extremely premature infants and greater recognition of bronchopulmonary dysplasia, necrotizing enterocolitis, retinopathy of prematurity, brain injury and developmental impairment. Neonatal research is similarly moving from descriptive epidemiology and rescue therapy towards prediction, prevention, precision medicine and implementation science. The next decade should prioritize prevention of prematurity, precision sepsis management, respiratory and brain protection, nutrition and gut health, Kangaroo Mother Care, zero separation, artificial intelligence and predictive analytics, long-term outcomes and affordable innovations. The ultimate measure of neonatal care should move beyond survival to enabling every newborn to develop and reach their full potential.

title: A targeted stewardship intervention improves the adequacy of antipseudomonal therapy after implementation of the EUCAST 2019 clinical category redefinitions
journal: Eur J Clin Microbiol Infect Dis
abstract: To evaluate the adequacy of antipseudomonal therapy in hospitalised patients following implementation of the 2019 EUCAST clinical category redefinitions through a multidisciplinary strategy. A mixed-design study was conducted in a university hospital. Adult inpatients with documented Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection and available antimicrobial susceptibility and treatment data were included. Two study periods were defined: a pre-intervention retrospective/training period and a post-intervention period. Primary outcome was adequacy of antimicrobial therapy. Secondary outcomes included clinical and microbiological variables. A total of 169 patients were included (78 pre-intervention and 91 post-intervention). Median age was 69 years (IQR 60-79), Charlson comorbidity index 5 (IQR 3-7) and SOFA score 3 (IQR 2-5). Analyses were adjusted for baseline differences between groups. Adequacy of antipseudomonal therapy increased significantly after the intervention (25/78 vs 79/91, p < 0.001). Interrupted time analysis (ITS) showed the intervention was associated with a marked and statistically significant immediate increase in the adequacy of antipseudomonal therapy (OR, 13.13; 95% CI, 1.73-113.25; p=0.015) after adjustment for time, SOFA score and infection type; without increased meropenem use. No significant differences were observed in mortality, readmissions or survival. Despite higher baseline severity in the post-intervention group, length of hospital stay was significantly shorter (OR = 0.98, p < 0.05). A non-significant trend toward fewer acquired resistance mutations was observed, consistent with improved local antipseudomonal susceptibility. Implementation of the 2019 EUCAST clinical category redefinitions, supported by coordinated interventions from Microbiology and Infectious Diseases specialists, was associated with a marked improvement in adequate antipseudomonal therapy without increased meropenem use or adverse clinical outcomes. The trend toward reduced resistance emergence suggests this strategy is ecologically safe and sustainable.

title: Synergistic effect of zinc oxide nanoparticles and antibiotics: a strategy to combat bacterial resistance
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) continues to compromise the clinical utility of conventional antibiotics, highlighting the need for innovative adjuvant strategies. Zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO-NP) have gained attention due to their intrinsic antimicrobial properties and capacity to potentiate antibiotic activity through multimodal mechanisms. This scoping review systematically mapped current evidence on ZnO-NP with antibiotics combinations (ZnO-NP-antibiotic) following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Searches in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science identified 14 eligible studies. To ensure comprehensive coverage of the literature, an additional manual search was conducted using Google Scholar and the reference lists of the included studies, and 10 further articles were identified. In total, 24 articles are included in this scoping review. Most investigations relied on simple physical mixtures (n = 13); while fewer explored conjugation between ZnO-NP-antibiotic (n = 3); encapsulated systems (n = 4); or drug-loaded (n = 4). Better antimicrobial activity was consistently reported across multiple antibiotic classes. Although all studies evaluated planktonic activity, only 10 incorporated biofilm models. Notably, translational maturity remains limited: more than half of the studies (n = 14) did not include toxicity assessment, and safety evaluation was considered based on in vitro cytotoxicity assays (n = 5); in vivo investigations (n = 5) or Hen's Egg Test-Chorioallantoic Membrane (HET-CAM) (n = 1). These findings indicate that ZnO-NP-antibiotic systems remain predominantly in the early stages of development. Future progress will require standardized antibiofilm methodologies, systematic toxicological profiling, pharmacokinetic characterization, and mechanistic validation to establish reproducible structure-activity relationships. Addressing these translational and regulatory challenges will determine whether nanoparticle-mediated synergy can advance beyond a laboratory proof-of-concept toward clinically viable antimicrobial strategies.

title: Ion-doped multifunctional nanozymes for infected wound management: design strategies and functional applications
abstract: Infected wounds are difficult to treat because persistent bacterial colonization, chronic inflammation, and antibiotic resistance jointly impair tissue repair. Nanozymes offer high stability, tunable enzyme-like activity, and multifunctional integration, but single-function systems often cannot address the dynamically changing wound microenvironment.
