We used the EnteroBase core genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST) scheme and its associated Hierarchical Clustering algorithm, along with other genome-based bioinformatics approaches such as single nucleotide variant-based phylogenetic analyses, ResFinder, PlasmidFinder, and RefSeq genomes, to characterise population structure, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) prevalence, and differences in gene content among genetic lineages. We analysed 1320 S Napoli genomes, collected between April, 1945, and September 14, 2022, from human (n=1088, 82·4%) and non-human (n=232, 17·6%) sources in Italy (n=317, 24%), Switzerland (n=181, 13·7%), France (n=773, 58·5%), and Spain (n=48, 3·6%), confirming that the rising prevalence of S Napoli is driven by a single monophyletic serotype within cgMLST superlineage HC2000_1289. However, this serotype displays considerable genetic diversity (15 lineages falling into 12 HC900 clusters), strong spatial structuring, and a low frequency (2%) of AMR determinants. We also detected genetic introgression between S Napoli and the sympatric, closely related Salmonella enterica serotype Veneziana. Unlike successful non-typhoidal Salmonella serotypes, for which globalisation has had a homogenising effect, S Napoli forms distinct lineages isolated by geographical distance. This study suggests that the persistence of S Napoli as a geographically structured metapopulation, causing localised human infections, could reflect the natural ecology of Salmonella before the rise of agribusiness. Future research should investigate the environmental reservoirs and transmission pathways of S Napoli. title: Selective attenuation of wastewater resistomes and residual ARG-MGE co-occurrence in semi-arid lagoon-treated effluents
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs), mobile genetic elements (MGEs), and clinically relevant bacterial taxa are environmental-health concerns in wastewater-impacted ecosystems. However, the capacity of lagoon systems to attenuate these AMR-related signals before effluent discharge or reuse remains insufficiently characterized in semi-arid regions. Shotgun metagenomics was applied to 34 influent and treated-effluent samples collected approximately weekly during January-March 2025 from two Moroccan lagoon systems: Settat (urban, n = 18) and Ouled Said (rural, n = 16). TPM-normalized taxonomic, resistome, and mobilome profiles were analyzed using diversity metrics, PERMANOVA, differential-abundance testing, and correlation networks. Lagoon treatment produced site-dependent microbial restructuring, with a marked shift in Ouled Said (Aitchison PERMANOVA, R = 0.376, p = 0.002) but a weaker, non-significant shift in Settat (R = 0.125, p = 0.054). ESKAPE-associated bacteria declined from approximately 38% to 32% of CARD-annotated taxa but remained detectable in effluents. The resistome was broadly attenuated, but last-resort antibiotic resistance genes (LR-ARGs) responded unevenly: most mcr variants decreased by 82.4-89.9%, with significant reductions for several variants, whereas blaand tet(X) showed limited or non-significant reductions. The mobilome declined, although transposases and insertion sequences remained prominent. Network analysis indicated denser residual statistical ARG-MGE-taxa co-occurrence after treatment, without implying increased genetic mobility or HGT. Overall, the systems acted as selective, context-dependent barriers, reducing AMR-related burdens while retaining clinically relevant residual signals. The contrasting site responses indicate that treatment performance should not be assumed to be uniform across lagoon systems and support targeted effluent surveillance for safer discharge and reuse.

title: Long-term study on spatiotemporal prevalence, distribution, and diversity of clinically relevant and environmental Acinetobacter species in Canadian agricultural watersheds
abstract: This study, conducted between 2018 and 2024, expands upon prior research through a culture-based investigation of the spatiotemporal prevalence, distribution, and diversity of Acinetobacter species across nine sites in an agriculturally-dominated watershed in eastern Ontario, Canada. Spatial analyses revealed, compared to medium to large stream order sites and forested reference site, agricultural drainage ditches consistently displayed higher Acinetobacter prevalence, cell concentrations, and diversity, likely due to direct proximity to livestock farms. Summer exhibited the highest Acinetobacter abundance and diversity, a pattern potentially linked to elevated temperatures, water stagnation, and seasonal runoff. Species-level identification revealed the widespread and persistent detection of several human health-associated species, including A. baumannii and A. pittii. The association of Acinetobacter species with upstream urban and agricultural land uses suggests that anthropogenically influenced waters may serve as critical sources for the environmental dissemination of pathogenic Acinetobacter and antimicrobial resistance genes. Furthermore, environmental Acinetobacter species, such as A. calcoaceticus, A. guillouiae, A. johnsonii, and A. soli, may play underappreciated roles in gene transfer and infection risk. This first in-depth analysis of Acinetobacter species within an agricultural aquatic ecosystem, offering a foundation for future research into environmental reservoirs of potential human pathogens and the spatiotemporal factors shaping microbial populations.

Fates and characteristics of antibiotic resistance genes carried by viruses during a full-scale anaerobic sludge digestion
abstract: The transmission of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) mediated by viruses in sludge represents an emerging concern for antibiotic resistance dissemination. This study investigated the virus-carried ARGs (vARGs) profiles and potential risks in sludges collected from an entire anaerobic sludge digestion plant. A total of 79 unique vARGs spanning 10 antibiotic resistance classes were identified, with trimethoprim resistance genes being the most diverse. Although most vARGs (94.9%) exhibited low sequence similarity (<70%) to known ARGs, the representative functional validation showed that virus-carried dfr genes could confer trimethoprim resistance to Escherichia coli. Thermal hydrolysis reduced the levels and diversity of vARGs, whereas subsequent anaerobic digestion led to substantial enrichment. More than 90% of vARGs in sludge viromes were removed after all treatment processes, but a significant number of ARG-carrying viruses (10- 10VLPs/g) still remained in the final sludges. In the metagenomes, the levels of vARGs increased approximately 7-fold, suggesting that vARGs were more difficult to be moved than plasmid-associated ARGs and chromosome-associated ARGs. The host prediction suggested associations between some vARG-carrying viruses and potential pathogenic bacteria, which are worth further experimental validation. In summary, the persistence of vARGs in sludge remains a concern, even after the implementation of sludge treatment processes.

title: Repurposing Ionophores to Tackle Antimicrobial Resistance with a Focus on PBT2
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) remains a growing global health challenge. While resistant bacterial strains continue to emerge and spread, the development of new antibiotics has remained slow. This gap has increased interest in drug repurposing as a promising strategy to combat multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogens. Ionophores are a structurally diverse group of natural and synthetic compounds that transport ions across biological membranes. Many ionophores were originally developed and widely used for the prevention and treatment of coccidiosis, a common protozoan parasitic intestinal disease in poultry and livestock. Recent studies suggest that some ionophores inhibit bacterial growth directly or enhance the activity of existing antibiotics by perturbing bacterial metal homeostasis, inducing oxidative stress, disturbing membrane function and disrupting biofilms. Among these compounds, PBT2, an 8-hydroxyquinoline derivative with zinc/copper ionophore activity, is an important example. PBT2 acts principally as an antibiotic adjuvant, restoring the activity of conventional antibiotics against several MDR pathogens when combined with zinc. PBT2 also demonstrates narrow-spectrum bactericidal activity as a monotherapy against selected Gram-negative bacteria, including Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Neisseria meningitidis and Helicobacter pylori. PBT2 has prior human exposure from Phase II trials in neurodegenerative diseases, but its antibacterial pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics remain undefined. This review summarises the discovery, classification and repurposing of ionophores, and examines the antibacterial activities of PBT2 and its proposed mechanisms of action. Finally, we discuss the translational barriers to the clinical use of ionophores, including bacterial selectivity, resistance risk, toxicity and safety.

title: From individual-based models to macroscopic dynamics of antimicrobial resistance
abstract: We introduce and discuss a kinetic framework describing the time evolution of the statistical distributions of a population divided into the compartments of susceptible, infectious, recovered, and resistant in the presence of a microbial infection driven by susceptible-infectious interactions. Our main objective is to quantify the impact of excessive and inappropriate antimicrobial use, which accelerates the spread of resistance by enabling a fraction of infectious individuals to transition into the resistant compartment. The model consists of a system of Boltzmann-type equations capturing binary interactions between susceptible and infectious individuals, complemented by linear redistribution operators that represent recovery, the development of resistance, and reinfection processes. In the grazing-collision limit, we show that this Boltzmann system is well approximated by a system of coupled Fokker-Planck equations. This limiting description allows for a more tractable analysis of the dynamics, including the characterization of the long-time behavior of the population densities. Our analysis highlights how interaction terms drive the system toward a stable equilibrium and quantifies the effects of inappropriate antimicrobial use on the distribution of resistant individuals. Overall, the results offer a multi-scale perspective that bridges kinetic theory with classical epidemic modeling.

title: Exposure to the broad-spectrum disinfectant glutaraldehyde facilitates antibiotic resistance genes dissemination via plasmid-mediated conjugation
abstract: Plasmid-mediated conjugative transfer is a major driver of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) dissemination, posing serious risks to ecosystems and human health. Glutaraldehyde (GA), a widely used disinfectant, is increasingly detected in environmental matrices, raising emerging concerns regarding its potential to promote ARGs spread. However, whether GA influences plasmid transfer remains largely unknown. Here, we showed that environmentally relevant concentrations of GA (0.01-1 mg/L) significantly enhanced the conjugative transfer of the multidrug resistance plasmid pKJK5 across both intra- and inter-genus bacterial systems. GA increased transfer frequencies by up to 4.29-fold in pure cultures and 4.16-fold in wastewater microbial communities, facilitating ARGs dissemination to diverse taxa, including several opportunistic pathogens. Mechanistically, GA damaged the integrity of the cell membrane, induced ROS production and the SOS response, promoted cell motility and biofilm formation, and upregulated genes involved in ROS detoxification, SOS regulation, membrane permeability, and conjugation. Nontargeted metabolomics profiling and molecular docking further supported these observations. Our findings reveal a previously overlooked role of GA in accelerating ARGs dissemination and underscore the environmental risks posed by commonly used disinfectants in driving the spread of clinically relevant multidrug-resistant pathogens.

title: Three-dimensional microfluidic nanoprecipitation of zein-loaded polyethylene glycol poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) nanoparticles with sustained-release antibacterial activity
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance calls for innovative drug delivery strategies that enhance natural antibacterial agents while minimizing off-target toxicity. Most cationic antimicrobial nanocarriers rely on electrostatic membrane binding as a prerequisite for bactericidal activity, which may compromise biocompatibility through nonspecific interactions with host cells. Here, we propose a nanoparticle-bacterium contact-independent sustained-release antibacterial approach using zein-loaded PEG-PLGA nanoparticles fabricated via three-dimensional (3D) microfluidic nanoprecipitation. The optimized nanoparticles (112.3 ± 7.1 nm, -35.4 ± 4.1 mV, 8.4 ± 1.0% drug loading) exhibited excellent colloidal stability, attenuated burst release, prolonged sustained release, preserved zein's intrinsic antioxidant activity, and supported favorable hemocompatibility and low cytotoxicity. Antibacterial assays revealed significantly enhanced activity against Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) (minimal inhibitory concentration, MIC 1.0 mg/mL, minimum bactericidal concentration, MBC 2.0 mg/mL) and Escherichia coli (E. coli) (MIC 1.5 mg/mL, MBC 3.0 mg/mL) versus free zein. Three independent lines of evidence supported the proposed nanoparticle-bacterium contact-independent sustained-release antibacterial mechanism. Scanning electron microscopy showed dose-dependent bacterial membrane rupture, while zeta potential measurements revealed no change in bacterial surface charge, indicating no detectable electrostatic adsorption. Propidium iodide uptake assays further demonstrated membrane permeabilization of approximately 50% at MIC and over 85% at MBC. Blank nanoparticles caused no membrane damage, suggesting that sustained drug liberation from the non-adherent carrier is a major contributor. This work provides evidence that potent antibacterial activity can occur without detectable electrostatic membrane adsorption under the tested conditions, offering a differentiated design principle for next-generation antibacterial nanomedicines.

title: Aptamer-Functionalized Pro-Photosensitizers for Targeted Elimination of Drug-Resistant Bacterial Biofilm Infection by Sequentially Activated Photodynamic-Antibiotic Therapy
abstract: Drug-resistant bacterial infections seriously threaten public health, and the formation of a biofilm barrier plays an important role. Drug-resistant biofilms are difficult to remove because the penetration and specificity of traditional antimicrobial drugs are poor, and the microenvironment in the inner layer of biofilms is hypoxic. Herein, we developed activatable aptamer-functionalized pro-photosensitizers (APMB) by modifying the clinical photosensitizer methylene blue (MB) with an aptamer that can specifically bind to drug-resistant bacteria. The APMB can simultaneously achieve imaging-guided efficient anti-infection and biofilm destruction, thereby increasing the therapeutic efficiency of the treatment of bacterial biofilm infections. Additionally, we co-loaded APMB and the antibiotic metronidazole (MNZ) into hydrogels to prepare a degradable microneedle patch, which can utilize photodynamic effects to eliminate biofilms under normoxic conditions and potentiate the hypoxic microenvironment to activate the antibacterial activity of MNZ, ultimately resulting in the synergistic killing of deep-seated bacteria. To summarize, this simple and intelligent phototheranostic molecular platform improves deep anti-infection efficacy through the synergistic effect of sequential activation while decreasing systemic toxicity, thereby providing a promising avenue for clinical translation to combat antimicrobial resistance.

title: A Selective Bis-Catecholate Siderophore-Ampicillin Conjugate Expands Activity against Multidrug-Resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a global public health crisis, with multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa among the most critical threats. The high cost and slow pace of novel antibiotic development, coupled with rapid resistance evolution, demand innovative strategies. Here, we present a Trojan horse approach using siderophore-antibiotic conjugates (SACs) to hijack bacterial iron uptake systems and deliver β-lactam payloads across the Gram-negative outer membrane. We designed a series of ampicillin conjugates with mono-catecholate, bis-catecholate, and catecholate-hydroxamate siderophores. These conjugates demonstrate potent antimicrobial activity. Notably, the lead compound, BC-2-Amp, shows broad-spectrum and highly selective activity against a panel of 105 clinical isolates of P. aeruginosa. Mechanistic studies demonstrated that BC-2-Amp utilizes PiuA as a critical receptor for targeted delivery. Complementary in vivo experiments further confirmed its promising therapeutic efficacy. Collectively, these findings establish SACs as a potent strategy for broadening the spectrum of β-lactam antibiotics and provide a robust platform for high-potency drug delivery.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is progressively undermining the efficacy of conventional antibiotics, and intracellular infections caused by Salmonella typhimurium (ST) remain difficult to eradicate, underscoring the need for alternative therapeutic strategies. To identify natural small molecules possessing both antivirulence and host-directed activities against ST infection, and further characterize their mechanisms of action. A dual-screening strategy was employed to identify compounds that inhibit both ST invasion and intracellular replication. RNA sequencing, quantitative polymerase chain reaction, western blot analysis, β-galactosidase reporter assay, scanning electron microscopy, and flow cytometry were performed to investigate the mode of action of the active compound. A murine enterocolitis model was established to evaluate its therapeutic efficacy. Ferulic acid (FA) emerged as a dual-acting inhibitor. FA suppressed SPI-4 promoter PsiiA activity, reduced SPI-4 transcription and SiiE secretion, and impaired SiiE-dependent adhesion, thereby limiting bacterial invasion. In parallel, FA suppressed macrophage STAT3 phosphorylation and enhanced NRF2 signaling, leading to reduced intracellular ferrous iron and ferroptosis, which in turn restricted intracellular bacterial replication. Furthermore, FA treatment alleviated ST-induced enterocolitis in mice. FA protects against ST infection by attenuating bacterial virulence and modulating host iron homeostasis. These findings support its potential as a combined antivirulence and host-directed therapeutic candidate.
